cells.tense: You're here, hands in the soil, tending what you actually want.
cells.verb: keeping two living things alive at once without starving either
cells.place: in the pull toward what you genuinely long for
cells.ask: let one person see what you've grown, and let that seeing count as done — so the care keeps its ease and the holding never turns into clutching
cells.core:
You're here, hands in the soil, tending what you actually want. The longing isn't a daydream to you and it isn't a burden either — it gets water, it gets a shape, it gets your attention on a schedule. And you're keeping more than one thing alive without letting one choke the other, which is the part most people can't do.

What this is free to feed next: let one person see what you've grown, and let their seeing count as finished. Not for applause — so that something gets to be done, set down, and left to stand on its own. The care stays light that way. The holding never has to turn into a grip.
cells.sheetLine: You're tending what you want, and nothing's being choked out.

cells.tense: You're tending toward a harvest that hasn't come, and can't be guaranteed.
cells.verb: managing what grows so hard the growing can't breathe
cells.place: in the pull toward what you genuinely long for
cells.ask: spend one evening on what has already come of it — feeling it fully, fixing nothing — until the wanting comes back as something you hold rather than something you grip
cells.core:
You're tending toward a harvest that hasn't come, and can't be guaranteed. Every stake, every pruning, every check on the weather is aimed at a future where the thing you want finally arrives safe — and the checking has become the whole relationship with it. What you long for is being managed instead of grown.

The way back isn't less care. It's letting yourself take in what's already come of this — one evening with what's already arrived, felt all the way through, with nothing to fix. Growth happens without forcing when the one tending it has actually tasted what grew. The wanting comes back as something you hold, not something you hold onto.
cells.sheetLine: You're managing the longing so closely it can't grow.

cells.tense: You're still standing at the gate of a garden you stopped going into.
cells.place: in the pull toward what you genuinely long for
cells.ask: take one step toward it that doesn't depend on how the last attempt went — keep walking at the star rather than back at the plot — and the tending returns on its own, as care that doesn't exhaust
cells.core:
You're still standing at the gate of a garden you stopped going into. The wanting didn't leave — you can feel the pull plain enough — but you stopped giving it water, shape, a day on the calendar. Somewhere back there, caring for it felt like it cost too much, and the hands came off.

Don't try to force your way back into the tending. Feed the other half: keep walking toward it. One step that doesn't depend on how the last one went, one step taken because the pull is still there after everything. That's where the strength comes from, and the care follows the walking. Holding returns as something that doesn't exhaust you.
cells.sheetLine: You still want it. You just stopped tending it.

cells.tense: You're already tending this, pen down, calling it chores.
cells.verb: keeping what grows alive without admitting it's yours
cells.place: in the pull toward what you genuinely long for
cells.ask: say to one person, out loud, that the thing you keep up is yours and you want it — so the tending can be held openly instead of carried quietly
cells.core:
You're already tending this, pen down, calling it chores. The time, the money, the small daily upkeep you give to one thing in particular — that's care for what you long for, and it's working. But you'd describe it as obligation, as something that has to get done, as anything but wanting.

The simpler move underneath all this: say it plainly to one person. That this thing you keep up is yours, and you want it. Let the wanting be seen once. What's tended in the open can be held with an easy hand; what's tended in secret has to be clutched.
cells.sheetLine: You're already caring for what you want. You call it upkeep.
